title: Mother of man slain at Sask. Pen opens up new $14.45M legal front against Alberta health officials, Calgary police
subtitle: The mother and brother of a man who died in custody at the Saskatchewan Penitentiary in 2017 say that his parole shouldn't have been suspended because of a drug overdose since it happened after the Good Samaritan Overdose Act was passed.
article: Lauren Laithwaite says none of the health or law enforcement authorities who came into contact with her son Chris Van Camp followed a law she argues in a new statement of claim would have prevented him from being put in custody at the Saskatchewan Penitentiary, where he died in June 2017.
Weeks before Van Camp died in custody, The Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act was passed on May 4, 2017.

As per the wording of the law, the act can protect people from charges related to possessing a controlled substance, or from breach of conditions regarding simple possession in pre-trial release, probation orders, conditional sentences and parole.

Van Camp, on parole in the spring of 2017, overdosed on fentanyl-laced cocaine and ended up in a coma for five days. When he awoke, officers with the Calgary Police Service executed a warrant for his arrest and he was soon returned to the Correctional Service of Canada's custody.

"You would think that people at this level of health care and justice, one person would have intervened to say 'Hey, this shouldn't be happening,' " Laithwaite said in an interview with the StarPhoenix on Monday evening. "Nobody did."
Laithwaite and her younger son, Ronald Lee Hopkins are seeking about $14.45 million in damages related to Van Camp's death.

In a statement of claim filed Jan. 31 through the Court of Queen's Bench in Calgary naming the Attorney General of Canada which represents the Correctional Service of Canada, Alberta Health Services and Foothills Medical Centre and the City of Calgary and Calgary Police Service, Laithwaite and her younger son, Ronald Lee Hopkins, allege the defendants should have or ought to have known the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act "provides immunity to those seeking medical attention in the event of drug overdose, even when that overdose is otherwise a violation of the person's parole."

The claim alleges that Van Camp was falsely imprisoned by the CSC and Calgary police on the basis his parole suspension on the grounds he failed to abstain from substance use was "unlawful and contrary" to the Act.
None of the claims have been proven in court.

On May 24, 2017, Van Camp was taken to Foothills Medical Centre, where he was in a coma for five days. On May 29, Calgary Police Service executed a warrant for his arrest on a breach of condition stemming from the overdose.

Van Camp was returned to CSC custody and taken to the Saskatchewan Penitentiary, located in Prince Albert. He was found unresponsive in his cell early on June 7. His cellmate, Tyler Vandewater was charged with second-degree murder.
According to a Parole Board of Canada report issued in December 2017 denying Vandewater parole, Van Camp had been found beaten, stabbed, wrapped in bags and blankets.
The claim alleges the Alberta Health Services and Foothills Medical Centre failed to ensure the authorities taking custody of Van Camp, their patient, had the legal authority to do so.

"In the absence of such authority, they had a duty to refuse to allow CPS officers to guard Chris, cuff him to his bed, or discharge him into CSC's custody. By complying with the unlawful arrest warrant, AHS and FMC breached their fiduciary duty to protect their patient, Chris, from false arrest and false imprisonment," the claim stated.
The defendants have 20 days to respond to the claim in Alberta.
She did not learn of the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act until three months after her son died.

Laithwaite filed an initial lawsuit, naming the federal attorney general representing the CSC, alleging corrections denied her son his Charter right to life and security by putting him in the same cell with Vandewater and that her son was in poor health and should not have been returned to custody. The case is still before the courts.

In January, Laithwaite attended Vandewater's most recent parole hearing, which took place in Saskatchewan. She plans to attend a trial as well as Vandewater's future parole hearings. She has decided not to attend any further court appearances until trial because the experience to be so emotionally draining that it took her a week to get grounded again.
"I needed to be in the room with him because I needed to sense what kind of man he was," she said.
Vandewater's case has been adjourned to March 15 at the Court of Queen's Bench in Prince Albert.
